His spine bowed in an arc as he crashed back against the tile, backlit by flickers of arc-light. Every nerve still screamed, but the body that should have obeyed them didn’t exist for a breathless second. Only pressure. A single, endless tone drilled through his skull while the rest of the world receded partially. He didn’t lose consciousness so much as slide away from it — a slow, drowning descent he fought the entire way. Muscles twitched in defiance, random surges of strength trying to pull him upright. The virus kept firing, desperate to restore order, burning through what oxygen remained. His chest convulsed once, twice. Uncoordinated limbs trying to push him upright, only to find their nerve signals either rerouted or straight up missing. Somewhere above the god-awful ringing through his head, something ticked. Bootsteps, measured and calm. A soft crackle of static answered by the scrape of a metal instrument tray. He couldn’t see through the spots of white and black, vague sharp scents driving through the haze in the few stuttering breaths he managed — ozone, antiseptic, faint alcohol on a gloved hand. His hearing staggered back one layer at a time; first the hiss of air vents, then a voice, blurred by distance but unmistakable in tone. The world tilted in stuttering frames. His vision crawled back by degrees, a film of static peeling off the edges. Cold. Steel walls. Shadows moving with precision instead of panic. The Fog’s usual hum had changed; it carried a rhythm now, electrical, surgical. He forced air into his lungs. It scraped raw, but it came. His hand twitched, scraping against the tile, fingers trying to curl. Move. His muscles spasmed instead, half-fire, half-failure. Uroboros thrashed under the skin, black veins splitting and healing in the same breath. The infection wanted to fight. His body wanted to obey. But the signals were wrong — every nerve fired out of order. A cold fingertip pressed against the inside of his wrist. Counting, clinical. Then a small, pleased hum. “Remarkable," Herman murmured, crouching beside him. "Even subdued, your resistance is impressive. The Fog nearly reclaimed you before I could stabilize the dose." Wesker’s head jerked toward the sound, the motion sending vertigo knifing through him. He caught the briefest shape — the outline of a gas mask, white coat, gleam of metal — and tried to stand anyway. His knees obeyed a moment too late, his own momentum collapsing him forward onto his palms. His body shook with the effort, sweat and blood mingling in neat drops across the floor. “Persistent,” Herman mused, “But predictable.” Wesker forced breath through clenched teeth, lips twitching into a snarl. “You... dare—” Herman stood, baton humming to life with a lazy flick of his thumb. “I do.” The air vibrated. Ozone filled the gap between them. “Stay down,” he advised softly. The next arc landed square across Wesker’s back. White fire. Every muscle seized, diaphragm locked against a pained scream. The current held for a full three seconds. Long enough for the virus to thrash against itself, for his vision to splinter again into black and gold, for strength to become convulsion. When it finally cut, he was on the floor again, chest heaving, body trembling in the aftermath. Nerves sang, muscles flickered in uncoordinated spasms, Uroboros retreating deep into the bone to survive the assault. Herman crouched nearby, studying the aftermath with professional satisfaction. The gloved hand returned to the wrist once more, counting beats. Steady enough now. Controlled. “Even now, the synaptic recovery is extraordinary. You’re actually still aware, aren’t you? Well, I can’t have you getting up too soon.” Herman loomed overhead, fog coiling around his ankles as the baton rose for a final, surgical strike. The blow landed with intent, just enough to make sure Wesker’s next memory would begin somewhere else. White swallowed everything. He surfaced slowly, dragged upward through the sludge of unconsciousness. Sparks still danced behind his eyelids, mingling with a throb through his skull that threatened to take him back under. The chemical tang clung thick in his throat, every breath laced with metal and smoke. His muscles twitched without command — phantom echoes of the shocks that had put him down. When his vision cleared, he wasn’t in the trial. He was sprawled on the cold steel of the station floor. He pushed himself upright with effort, balance wavering. Every muscle felt wrong. Slow. Re-synced. One hand pressed to his head, trying to settle the residual spinning from the toxin that hadn’t quite finished clearing from his system yet. The movement set off a sharp sting in his wrist, as if something had cut into him. His eyes dropped to the offending limb. A sleek, black band, fused around his wrist like a parasite. No latch. No weld. It pulsed faintly against his skin, like it was breathing with him. Or against him. The metal laid flush against his skin, and attempting to rotate it in place sent a sharp stab straight to the bone. The band had teeth, at least some long enough to reach down through muscle, grazing bone and anchoring it in place. Embedded. Wesker curled his fingers, flexing against the band, pulsing his virus against it. Pain. Searing. Sharp. Immediate. Agony punched through him, dropping him to one knee before he could prepare, vision scattering in a haze of static. Overhead, an intercom speaker crackled, the Doctor’s chuckles bleeding through the walls. “Well, now that IS a strong reaction. Let me jot that down.” Wesker snarled at the voice, the intrusion on the only place in this cursed Fog that was his alone.
